question: Can information be decomposed, relative to a computationally bounded observer, into learnable structure and irreducible uncertainty, and can that decomposition be estimated from neural-network learning curves to compare algorithms, factorizations, datasets, and data-selection rules?

key_findings.claim: The paper defines epiplexity and time-bounded entropy through a two-part, time-bounded probabilistic-program code, so both quantities are observer-, time-budget-, and description-language-relative rather than intrinsic constants of a dataset.
key_findings.evidence: For programs whose sampling and probability evaluation fit a time budget T, the selected program P* minimizes |P| plus expected negative log probability. Epiplexity S_T is |P*| and time-bounded entropy H_T is the remaining expected log loss. The paper explicitly frames the split as relative to a bounded observer and notes dependence on the universal machine up to coding constants.

key_findings.claim: Cryptographically secure pseudorandom-generator output can look maximally unpredictable to polynomial-time observers while having a short bounded program, formally separating time-bounded entropy from epiplexity.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 9 gives H_poly(G(U_k)) at least n minus a negligible term and S_poly(G(U_k)) at most a constant plus a negligible term for a length-expanding secure PRG. Appendix B reduces a non-negligible log-loss advantage over uniform to a polynomial-time distinguisher and constructs the short sampler/evaluator program.

anchors.section: Appendix B.1 Pseudorandomness and Time-Bounded Entropy
Appendix B.1 Proof of Epiplexity Bound

key_findings.claim: The manuscript's statement that H(G(U_k)) equals k silently needs injectivity of G; the stated PRG definition does not impose injectivity.
key_findings.evidence: Definition 3 only requires a polynomial-time length-expanding map whose output is computationally indistinguishable from uniform. For a deterministic map, Shannon entropy H(G(U_k)) is at most k and equals k only when seeds have distinct outputs. The later exact equality is therefore not established from the definition as written, although secure expansion can still support near-maximal computational entropy and collisions can be constrained by security.

key_findings.claim: A deterministic efficient transformation can raise time-bounded entropy by almost n-k bits, so a computational data-processing inequality need not hold.
key_findings.evidence: For X uniform on k bits and a secure length-expanding PRG G, Theorem 12/18 compares the trivially encoded input with G(X): ordinary entropy cannot increase, but polynomial-time entropy rises from at most k to at least n minus a negligible term. The result is conditional on the security assumption and the selected polynomial observer class.

anchors.section: 5.1 Deterministic Computation Can Increase Entropy / Theorem 12
Appendix B.2 Failure of Data Processing / Theorem 18

key_findings.claim: Under one-way-function assumptions there are distribution families with growing epiplexity, but the proved lower bound is only logarithmic and existential.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 10 states that one-way functions imply ensembles with S_poly(X_n)=Omega(log n). The appendix builds a family from pseudorandom functions and uses a counting/diagonalization argument over short time-bounded programs. It does not construct a natural high-epiplexity dataset or prove the much larger empirical magnitudes inferred later.

anchors.section: Appendix B.3 High Epiplexity from Pseudorandom Functions

key_findings.claim: A one-way permutation yields a directional factorization gap and a failure of a time-bounded Bayes identity.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 13/25 compares Y=f(X) with X uniform: predicting Y from X is efficient whereas predicting X from Y would invert f, producing an omega(log n) asymmetry between the two chain-rule-style factorizations. Corollary 26 turns this into a violation of the corresponding Bayes equality. These are conditional asymptotic results for the formal bounded-program measure, not proofs that rule 30 or chess is one-way.

key_findings.claim: The prequential area-above-final-loss estimator is explicitly a heuristic rather than a certified upper bound on epiplexity.
key_findings.evidence: The estimator subtracts the final-model loss from a sequence of prequential coding losses. The authors acknowledge that subtracting two upper bounds is not generally an upper bound, that time-bounded symmetry-of-information arguments are unavailable, and that the approximation assumes small generalization gaps and adequate convergence. It can therefore inherit optimization, overfitting, and checkpoint-choice artifacts.

key_findings.claim: Requential coding supplies a more explicit teacher/student code, but the reported practical quantity drops coding overheads and depends on replaying a chosen training algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: The construction transmits relative-entropy samples from successive students with a bound of KL plus log(1+KL)+4 bits, while experiments approximate this by KL alone. The decoder replays training and the paper budgets about 6ND training FLOPs plus 2N times test-set inference, while acknowledging a practical 2-10x slowdown. Relative-entropy decoding and communication work are not included in the headline 6ND accounting.

key_findings.claim: The empirical estimator is a model-family and optimization frontier, not a direct optimizer over all bounded programs.
key_findings.evidence: For each number of training examples/tokens, the implementation sweeps model sizes and hyperparameters, retains the lower convex hull of loss versus training FLOPs, and selects a median checkpoint. Teacher/student KL uses EMA models and maximum-over-checkpoint safeguards. These defensible engineering choices make the estimate conditional on architectures, schedules, seeds, and sweep coverage.

anchors.section: Appendix C.1 Lower Convex Hull and Checkpoint Selection

key_findings.claim: Elementary cellular automata qualitatively separate simple, pseudorandom-looking, and structured-hard conditional distributions under the neural estimator.
key_findings.evidence: Using 64-cell states, 48-step sequences after a 1,000-step burn-in, 100M test tokens, and width/depth sweeps, rule 15 has low estimated entropy and epiplexity, rule 30 high entropy but low epiplexity, and rule 54 intermediate entropy with high epiplexity. The result is a selected three-rule case study with no uncertainty intervals or proof that the trained family reaches the formal optimum.

key_findings.claim: Forward rule-30 evolution is estimated as easier than reverse reconstruction, but the experiment is an analogy to one-way computation rather than a cryptographic result.
key_findings.evidence: Models predicting the next rule-30 state have lower requential entropy/epiplexity than models predicting predecessors from successors. Rule 30 is not proved one-way, and reverse prediction may differ in ambiguity, context, and target entropy independently of computational inversion hardness.

key_findings.claim: Chess move-to-board and board-to-move factorizations differ in estimated code length and downstream behavior, but the paper reports no replicated uncertainty or causal isolation.
key_findings.evidence: Character models from roughly 1M to 160M parameters train for 5B tokens on Lichess representations. The reverse board-to-moves factorization has larger estimated entropy/epiplexity; forward-factorization models do better on 50,000 high-rated puzzles, while reverse models obtain lower centipawn error in a nine-bin board-evaluation task. Different serialization direction, ambiguity, truncation, and conditional target information can all contribute, and the figures provide no seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

key_findings.claim: Controlled induction studies support a non-monotone structural-cost story: hidden rule-30 steps become harder roughly exponentially, whereas partially hiding a finite Markov transition table creates an intermediate epiplexity peak.
key_findings.evidence: The hard task applies four rule-30 steps to 32-bit strings and hides h bits/steps; compute and estimated epiplexity rise strongly through h=5. The easy task samples from an 8-state random Markov matrix and hides rows; fully visible and fully resampled endpoints are simpler than intermediate partial structure. Both use one constructed task family and fixed small Transformers, so the shapes do not establish universal laws.

key_findings.claim: The rule-54 looped-model experiment shows a finite architecture-dependent phase change, not the asymptotic emergence property defined by the paper.
key_findings.evidence: A looped model predicting 16 intermediate states abruptly reduces MDL/estimated epiplexity at sufficient depth, while the direct model does not; only loop length 16 is advantageous. Definition 14 requires an asymptotic separation and nonempty emergence class, and the authors state that even Game of Life is not proved to satisfy it. The finite sweep is illustrative evidence compatible with brute-force computation, not a theorem about emergence.

key_findings.claim: The natural-data comparison ranks character text above chess and grayscale CIFAR pixels in estimated epiplexity, but representation and tokenization confound any modality-level conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: At a common plotted compute scale, OpenWebText filtered to 96 characters has the largest estimated structural component, Lichess is next, and grayscale CIFAR-5M pixels have the smallest structural fraction and over 99% estimated random content. A character, a chess serialization symbol, and an 8-bit grayscale pixel are not comparable information units; dataset scale, image resolution, preprocessing, architecture, and loss all differ. The experiment therefore measures these encodings under this model family, not an intrinsic text-versus-image hierarchy.

key_findings.claim: The natural-data token budget is internally inconsistent: the Figure 10 caption says 1B training tokens, while the surrounding text and appendix specify 5B.
key_findings.evidence: The body describes training the largest models for 5B tokens and Appendix C.3 repeats 5B, but the Figure 10 caption labels the estimates as 1B-token results. The discrepancy changes the practical code budget and prevents an exact reconstruction from the main figure alone.

anchors.section: 5.5 Natural Data / Figure 10 caption and body

key_findings.claim: The 1T-token, 10^25-FLOP modality comparison is an extrapolation assembled from external scaling laws rather than a direct requential-code experiment.
key_findings.evidence: The paper combines Chinchilla-style compute allocation with fitted language, image-token, raw-image, and video scaling curves, including embedding-cost corrections, to project epiplexity. The extrapolated ranking puts text highest, VQ-token images above raw pixels, and video lower. Cross-paper losses, token units, architectures, and scaling regimes are heterogeneous, so this supports a hypothesis rather than a controlled estimate.

key_findings.claim: The ADO analysis aligns data-selection gains with the proxy by construction and is not an independent intervention on epiplexity.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reanalyzes published 1.3B- and 125B-parameter Pile experiments in which ADO upweights domains with faster-decreasing validation loss. Such loss decrease is also the area accumulated by the prequential proxy, so ADO mechanically favors data scored as more learnable. Reported downstream and out-of-domain gains are useful external outcomes, but the study reuses prior runs and does not hold entropy, domain mix, or compute constant while directly manipulating epiplexity.

key_findings.claim: The paper correctly limits epiplexity's downstream interpretation: structural learnability alone does not guarantee usefulness for a particular task or out-of-distribution generalization.
key_findings.evidence: The introduction distinguishes broad learnable structure from task-relevant information, and the chess discussion notes that factorization-specific pretraining helps matching downstream tasks rather than every task. This qualification is important because the estimator is unconditional or next-token predictive MDL, not a causal measure of semantic value.

key_findings.claim: The claimed universal collapse of naive time-bounded sophistication is directionally plausible but its proof sketch does not establish the lemma exactly as stated.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix proposes a clocked interpreter that recovers the output length n and enforces t(n), then says sophistication is O(1) for every significance c at least zero. The described decoder receives only the data part d, so obtaining the relevant output length before simulating is not specified; moreover the constant clock/interpreter program need not fit every c, especially c=0. A revised encoding or significance threshold could repair the idea, but the stated construction omits those budget details.

anchors.section: Appendix B.5 Lemma and Proof Sketch

key_findings.claim: The asymptotic convergence argument for the empirical optimizer needs stronger regularity than the pointwise loss convergence and unique limiting minimizer stated in the proof.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B.4.3 argues that D*(T) converges to D_test because each fixed distribution's bounded loss converges and the limiting objective has a unique minimizer. Pointwise convergence alone does not generally imply convergence of argmin sequences over a changing or noncompact candidate set; uniform convergence, compactness/equicoercivity, and separation of the minimizer would be sufficient kinds of additions. Thus the proposition's proof has a formal gap as written.

anchors.section: Appendix B.4.3 Convergence of the Optimal Training Distribution

key_findings.claim: The formal optimization does not force a program to replay neural training, whereas the practical requential code does, leaving a gap between the definition's time accounting and the estimator's chosen code family.
key_findings.evidence: A time-bounded probabilistic program may directly contain learned parameters if their description fits the code-length objective; the practical code instead sends a training procedure and replays successive students. This is a valid candidate code and therefore an upper-bound-style construction, but it does not show that training replay is the optimal bounded program or that all model-acquisition compute is charged identically in the formal definition.

key_findings.claim: The empirical claims are largely point estimates from finite sweeps without seed-level uncertainty, making rank claims and abrupt transitions less secure than the plots suggest.
key_findings.evidence: Experimental appendices specify architectures, budgets, and optimizer settings but generally do not report independent seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or sensitivity to the model-family frontier. This is particularly consequential for the chess comparisons, emergence threshold, natural-modality ranking, and scaling-law extrapolations.

anchors.section: Appendix C.3 Natural Data and Chess

key_findings.claim: Lorenz-system and AlphaZero discussions are illustrative extensions, not controlled validations of the estimator's core claims.
key_findings.evidence: The Lorenz appendix uses predictability horizons to discuss observer-relative entropy in chaotic dynamics, while the AlphaZero section interprets self-play improvement through learnable novelty. Neither supplies the same explicit requential code, comparative baseline, replicated quantitative table, or causal test used in the main synthetic studies.

anchors.section: Appendix D.1 Chaotic Dynamics and Lorenz Systems

method.core_idea: Replace a single entropy number with a bounded two-part description: the shortest feasible generative/predictive program is learnable structure (epiplexity), while its residual expected log loss is bounded-observer uncertainty. Approximate that split with neural learning curves and an explicit sequence of trainable teacher/student codes.
method.mechanism: Formally minimize program length plus expected negative log likelihood over probabilistic programs that can sample and evaluate probabilities within T. Prove cryptographic separations, failure of computational data processing, existence of logarithmically growing epiplexity, and factorization asymmetry under standard assumptions. Practically, train model families at increasing token counts and compute either a prequential area above final loss or a requential sum of teacher/student KL costs; optimize the empirical compute/code frontier over model sizes, schedules, and checkpoints. Apply the estimates to cellular automata, constructed induction, chess factorizations, natural data, scaling-law projections, and an existing adaptive data-optimization study.
assumptions: A fixed universal coding language and time budget define the observer; absolute epiplexity values depend on that choice even when asymptotic statements tolerate constants.
The admissible program class supports both normalized sampling and probability evaluation within T.
The minimizer P* exists or an equivalent infimum/near-minimizer can stand in for it.
Cryptographic theorems assume secure PRGs, one-way functions, pseudorandom functions, or one-way permutations against the stated polynomial-time observer class.
The exact Shannon-entropy equality for PRG output additionally requires injectivity, which is not part of Definition 3 as written.
Neural architectures, optimizers, tokenizations, and hyperparameter sweeps approximate the relevant bounded-program frontier sufficiently well for empirical comparisons.
Teacher and student distributions are well calibrated enough that measured KL reflects code cost rather than only optimization or approximation error.
EMA teacher/student checkpoints and the maximum-KL safeguard provide a decodable progression representative of the intended code.
Dropping log(1+KL)+4 and implementation overhead from relative-entropy coding does not change qualitative rankings.
Training replay, relative-entropy decoding, and inference fit the selected practical time budget, despite additional wall-clock overhead.
Prequential estimation assumes small generalization gaps and treats a difference of coding-loss upper bounds as a useful proxy despite lacking a general bound.
The lower convex hull and median-checkpoint selection recover stable compute-efficient frontiers from finite runs.
Conditional serializations being compared expose comparable information and do not introduce dominant tokenization, ambiguity, or truncation artifacts.
Learning-curve extrapolations remain valid many orders of magnitude beyond or across the fitted regimes and across heterogeneous modality token units.
Estimated structural information is relevant to the downstream question being asked; epiplexity alone does not guarantee task-specific utility.

techniques.role: Defines the formal two-part program-plus-log-loss objective under bounded sampling and evaluation time.
Turns predictive/log-loss advantages into distinguishers to prove pseudorandomness and factorization separations.
Names the residual expected log loss of the optimal bounded program.
Names the code length of the optimal bounded program as learnable structural information.
Approximates structural code by the area of sequential learning loss above final-model loss.
Builds a replayable teacher/student code by summing KL-based costs across increasing training sets.
Selects model, token-count, and checkpoint combinations on a lower convex hull before estimating code length.
Stabilizes cross-scale model sweeps and teacher/student distributions in the practical estimator.
Provides controlled simple, pseudorandom-looking, asymmetric, and emergent-computation examples.
Compares forward and reverse conditional codes in rule 30 and chess.
Projects the learnable-structure area from published loss/compute curves at large budgets.

evaluations.setting: Elementary cellular automata rules 15, 30, and 54; 64 cells, 48-step sequences after 1,000 burn-in steps; width 16-512, depth 1-9 models; 100M test tokens
evaluations.metric: Requential estimates of time-bounded entropy and epiplexity
evaluations.result: Rule 15 is low entropy/low epiplexity, rule 30 high entropy/low epiplexity, and rule 54 intermediate entropy/high epiplexity; only plotted estimates are supplied.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-rule comparison under the same conditional-prediction pipeline

evaluations.setting: Rule-30 four-step induction on 32-bit inputs with h=0 through 5 hidden intermediate information units; 3-layer width-256 Transformer trained 20,000 steps
evaluations.metric: Compute to learn and estimated epiplexity as hidden computation increases
evaluations.result: The plotted compute and structural-code cost rise sharply, described as exponential in hidden computation; no fitted exponent, uncertainty, or alternative architecture test is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Fully exposed h=0 construction and smaller h settings

evaluations.setting: Eight-state random Markov transition matrix with varying numbers of hidden rows; 3-layer width-128 Transformer, sequence length 512, 3,000 steps
evaluations.result: Intermediate hiding produces the highest estimated structure, while the fully specified and effectively resampled endpoints are lower.
evaluations.baseline: Fully visible table and maximally hidden/resampled endpoints

evaluations.setting: Forward versus reverse rule-30 conditional prediction
evaluations.metric: Estimated conditional time-bounded entropy and epiplexity
evaluations.result: Reverse reconstruction is estimated to require more structure and residual loss than forward evolution.

evaluations.setting: Lichess character serializations, move-sequence-to-final-board versus final-board-to-move-sequence; about 1M-160M parameters and 5B training tokens
evaluations.metric: Requential entropy/epiplexity plus puzzle accuracy and nine-bin centipawn evaluation
evaluations.result: The reverse factorization has larger code components; forward models perform better on 50,000 high-rated puzzles and reverse models better on board-value prediction. Numeric tables and uncertainty are absent.
evaluations.baseline: Opposite chess factorization at matched reported model/token budgets

evaluations.setting: Rule-54 direct model versus a looped model trained to predict 16 intermediate states; width 16-128 and depth 1-32
evaluations.metric: MDL/requential epiplexity and loss across depth
evaluations.result: The looped model shows an abrupt drop at sufficient depth only for loop length 16, interpreted as transition to brute-force computation; the direct model does not show the same drop.
evaluations.baseline: Direct predictor and loop lengths other than 16

evaluations.setting: OpenWebText restricted to 96 characters, Lichess text, and grayscale CIFAR-5M pixels; model sizes up to about 160M and reported 5B-token training
evaluations.metric: Estimated epiplexity and residual random-information fraction near 6x10^18 FLOPs
evaluations.result: Text is ranked most structurally rich, chess next, images least; grayscale images are estimated above 99% random. Figure 10's caption instead says 1B tokens.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-modality comparison under modality-specific encodings and models

evaluations.setting: Published language, raw-image, VQ-image, and video scaling curves extrapolated to 1T tokens and 10^25 FLOPs
evaluations.metric: Projected epiplexity from area between finite- and large-budget loss curves
evaluations.result: Text is projected highest, tokenized images above raw pixels, and video lower; this is a heterogeneous cross-paper extrapolation rather than a direct experiment.
evaluations.baseline: The modalities' published loss-scaling fits after compute/token corrections

evaluations.setting: Reanalysis of Adaptive Data Optimization runs on the Pile at 1.3B and 125B model scales
evaluations.metric: Prequential epiplexity proxy, in-domain and out-of-domain loss, and downstream aggregate performance
evaluations.result: ADO-selected mixtures receive a higher learnable-structure proxy and previously reported downstream/OOD improvements; no new randomized intervention isolates epiplexity.
evaluations.baseline: Static data mixtures from the source ADO experiments

limitations: Author-stated: epiplexity is observer- and compute-relative and is not a universal, representation-free property of data.
Author-stated: the prequential difference is not a rigorous upper bound because it subtracts upper bounds and lacks a suitable bounded symmetry-of-information theorem.
Author-stated: practical requential coding is substantially slower than ordinary training and the implementation approximates the theoretical relative-entropy code.
Author-stated: high epiplexity does not by itself imply task relevance, semantic value, or out-of-distribution transfer.
Author-stated: the asymptotic emergence class is not proved nonempty for natural candidates such as Game of Life.
Reviewer: the empirical optimizer ranges over a narrow neural/code family, so its estimates need not approximate the formal minimum over bounded probabilistic programs.
Reviewer: most empirical comparisons lack seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, and sensitivity to the hyperparameter frontier.
Reviewer: the natural-modality ranking compares incompatible token units, encodings, dataset scales, objectives, and model inductive biases.
Reviewer: the scaling-law projection combines external fits across regimes and extrapolates to 10^25 FLOPs without uncertainty propagation.
Reviewer: factorization comparisons can be driven by conditional ambiguity, serialization, context length, and target entropy in addition to computational directionality.
Reviewer: the existential Omega(log n) theorem is much weaker than a characterization or lower bound for the natural datasets scored in the experiments.
Reviewer: universal-machine constants and the encoding of learned weights/training procedures matter at the finite scales where reported bit totals are interpreted.
failure_modes: The selected model family can underfit structure and misclassify learnable information as residual entropy.
An oversized or overfit final model can distort the prequential area, including making the difference unstable or negative on portions of a curve.
Teacher/student KL can reflect calibration, EMA, optimization, or support mismatch rather than only information acquired from added data.
Dropping relative-entropy coding overheads can change rankings when KL increments are small.
Finite hyperparameter sweeps and lower-hull selection can turn optimization luck into apparent code efficiency.
A supposedly pseudorandom natural process can contain exploitable structure outside the tested architecture or compute range.
Reverse tasks can be one-to-many, truncated, or encoded less efficiently, creating a factorization gap without one-way computational hardness.
The looped architecture can win because of supervision and inductive bias, while the observed finite jump is mistaken for an asymptotic emergence transition.
Cross-modality token counts can produce arbitrary rankings when a token carries different numbers and kinds of raw bits.
Data-selection methods that optimize learning-speed signals can appear validated by a proxy made from the same signal even without added causal structure.
The naive time-bounded-sophistication decoder cannot enforce the claimed output-length-dependent clock without an adequate encoding of length and interpreter budget.
Pointwise convergence of objectives can permit wandering minimizers, invalidating the stated optimal-training-distribution convergence argument.
PRG entropy can be below seed entropy when the generator is noninjective, contradicting exact equalities that assume otherwise.
A structural-information proxy can reward easily learned artifacts, memorization, leakage, or spurious regularities that do not help the intended downstream task.
reusable_insights: Report model-description or acquisition cost separately from irreducible predictive log loss; a single compression number hides whether improvement came from learned structure or residual fit.
Treat every practical MDL estimate as relative to an explicit architecture, optimizer, tokenizer, compute budget, and decoder protocol.
Use cryptographic indistinguishability to construct clean examples where statistical entropy and computational predictability diverge.
Audit both directions of a factorization because bounded conditional descriptions need not obey classical chain-rule intuition.
Prefer an explicit decodable teacher/student code when possible, and itemize rather than discard its training, decoding, inference, and communication overheads.
Use lower-envelope learning curves to compare code efficiency, but accompany frontier selection with seed/bootstrap uncertainty and held-out architecture families.
Normalize cross-modality comparisons in raw bits, examples, or calibrated rate-distortion units rather than calling heterogeneous symbols equal tokens.
Separate asymptotic definitions from finite phase-transition evidence and state which one an experiment actually establishes.
Validate a learnability-derived data score against interventions or outcomes not mechanically computed from the same loss-decrease curve.
Proof audits of argmin convergence should check uniformity, compactness/equicoercivity, and minimizer separation rather than relying on pointwise convergence.
open_questions: Can epiplexity be estimated with certified upper and lower bounds for useful nontrivial program classes rather than a heuristic neural frontier?
How sensitive are empirical values and rankings to universal-language choice, architecture, optimizer, tokenizer, random seed, and allowed wall-clock budget?
Can relative-entropy coding be implemented end to end with measured bits and decoding time, including every overhead in the formal budget?
What sufficient conditions repair the optimal-training-distribution convergence theorem, and do the empirical model families satisfy them?
Can the time-bounded-sophistication collapse be restated with an explicit self-delimiting length code and a valid significance threshold?
Do natural tasks exhibit provable factorization asymmetry without importing cryptographic assumptions, and can ambiguity be separated from hardness?
Is there a controlled natural system that satisfies the paper's asymptotic definition of computational emergence?
Does estimated epiplexity predict downstream transfer after controlling for entropy, domain, representation, dataset size, and model-data alignment?
Can modality comparisons be made under a shared rate-distortion target and uncertainty-calibrated scaling law?
Would a randomized data-selection intervention targeting epiplexity outperform learning-speed, diversity, or domain-match controls at equal compute?
How should finite-data stochastic complexity and parameter precision be incorporated when the program can either store weights or replay training?
Can a task-conditional or causal epiplexity distinguish robust structure from shortcuts and memorized artifacts?

competitive_landscape.title: A Theory of Usable Information Under Computational Constraints
competitive_landscape.difference: Predictive V-information/V-entropy already makes information relative to a constrained predictive family and shows familiar information laws can fail. It is task/label conditioned and does not split dataset information into a bounded program description plus residual entropy; the target's novelty is the program-MDL decomposition and cryptographic/empirical development, not the general idea of observer-relative usable information.

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring Information Transfer in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This work uses prequential coding to quantify information transfer from representations and models. It closely precedes the target's practical area-above-loss logic, but does not define a formal time-bounded random-versus-structural decomposition or an explicit requential teacher/student code.

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluating Representations by the Complexity of Learning Low-Loss Predictors
competitive_landscape.relationship: sample-complexity and description-length competitor for usable structure
competitive_landscape.difference: Surrogate description length evaluates how quickly low-loss task predictors can be learned from a representation. It is downstream-task conditional and rewards lower learning complexity, whereas the target interprets a larger learned dataset code as more structural information and separately accounts for residual uncertainty.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Modeling Is Compression
competitive_landscape.difference: Delétang et al. evaluate language models as compressors for text, images, and audio and establish broad empirical links between prediction and compression. They measure total compression under pretrained models, not a time-bounded separation between program/training cost and irreducible data entropy; their cross-modal results also underscore representation-normalization issues for the target's modality claims.

competitive_landscape.title: Compute-Optimal LLMs Provably Generalize Better With Scale
competitive_landscape.relationship: same-line theoretical competitor connecting compute, quantization, information, and generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: This work proves generalization behavior for compute-optimal language models through information/precision arguments. It concerns trained-model generalization under scaling rather than an intrinsic bounded-observer decomposition of a data distribution, but it supplies a more direct generalization target than treating high epiplexity as broadly useful.

competitive_landscape.title: The Size of Teachers as a Measure of Data Complexity: PAC-Bayes Excess Risk Bounds and Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Teacher size near a target risk is used as a task-specific data-complexity measure with PAC-Bayes excess-risk bounds and scaling laws. The target instead counts a bounded generative/predictive program and residual log loss, including a training-replay code; it offers a structural/random split but lacks the competitor's direct risk-bound interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Curve Theory
competitive_landscape.relationship: theoretical competitor for interpreting and extrapolating learning curves
competitive_landscape.difference: Viering and Loog study mechanisms and variability that can generate diverse learning-curve shapes. That work does not propose an information decomposition, but it cautions against treating finite power-law curves as a uniquely identified structural code and supplies alternative explanations for the target's scaling extrapolations.

competitive_landscape.title: Intelligence from Learnable Novelty
competitive_landscape.relationship: current direct successor and operational competitor
competitive_landscape.difference: This later work operationalizes learnable novelty with cheaper reservoir/ridge estimators and objectives in cellular automata, representation learning, and reinforcement learning. It narrows any current claim that the target uniquely introduces learnable structural information; the target remains earlier and distinctive in its formal bounded-program MDL split, cryptographic proofs, and requential coding construction.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a new information-theoretic quantity, epiplexity, that captures learnable structural information available to a computationally bounded observer while separating it from time-bounded entropy; they claim formal cryptographic separations, failures of data processing and Bayes/chain-rule intuitions, a computable neural requential estimator, and evidence that the quantity explains algorithmic emergence, factorization, natural-data differences, scaling, and adaptive data selection.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact indexed 65-page revision defines a bounded probabilistic-program MDL objective, proves conditional PRG/PRF/one-way-permutation theorems, constructs prequential and KL-based requential estimators, and applies them across cellular automata, synthetic induction, chess, text/images, cross-paper scaling fits, and prior ADO runs. It also explicitly acknowledges that the prequential proxy is not a bound, downstream value is task dependent, and the asymptotic emergence example is unproved.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest defensible novelty is the particular two-part time-bounded probabilistic-program definition together with its cryptographic separation results and an unusually broad attempt to operationalize the split through a replayable teacher/student code. Observer-relative usable information, resource-bounded Kolmogorov/MDL ideas, prequential information, learning-curve complexity, prediction-as-compression, and teacher-size data complexity all predate it. Current follow-on work also offers cheaper learnable-novelty operationalizations. The formal contribution should be stated with caveats: the PRG Shannon-entropy equality needs injectivity, the naive time-bounded-sophistication lemma omits length/significance details, and the argmin-convergence proof needs uniformity or compactness conditions. Empirical novelty is hypothesis-generating rather than validating a universal measure because values depend on a finite neural/code frontier, most results lack uncertainty, one token-budget caption conflicts with the setup, modality comparisons are not normalized, and ADO shares the proxy's learning-speed signal. Confidence is therefore high on what the paper defines and reports, moderate on formal completeness, and moderate-low on broad causal interpretations.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review of the exact indexed arXiv:2601.03220v2 PDF (current official revision dated 2026-03-16).
